title: The cognitive neuroscience of auditory distraction
review_question: What are the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying auditory distraction's disruption of working memory, particularly focusing on the role of prefrontal cortex?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The review focuses on recent PET experiments by Gisselgård et al. [3,4] as a 'major development' in understanding auditory distraction, integrating these findings with broader cognitive and neuroscientific literature on working memory and attention.

findings.antecedent: Change within ignored distracting sound (changing-state sequence of sounds, e.g., ABAB...)
findings.quote: Change within the ignored distracting sound has been pinpointed as a key determinant of disruption of working memory by auditory distraction ([5,6], see also [7]).

findings.consequent: involuntary processing, which disrupts the processing of to-be-remembered material
findings.quote: To explain this changing-state effect, cognitive theory has invoked the concept of an involuntary processing of ignored changing-state material, which disrupts the processing of the to-be-remembered material [5].

findings.antecedent: Ignored changing-state speech sound during an easy working-memory task (6 digits)
findings.consequent: deactivation (suppression) of left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, bilateral secondary auditory cortex, and left inferior parietal cortex, leading to unaffected working-memory performance
findings.quote: Changing-state material resulted in a suppression of several brain areas, crucially involving left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and brain regions implicated in the temporary storage of speech-based material... so successfully ignored that sound such that working-memory performance was unaffected.

findings.antecedent: Ignored changing-state speech sound during a difficult working-memory task (8 digits)
findings.consequent: activation of the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex and disruption of working-memory performance
findings.quote: The additional demands of the task recruited the involvement of the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex on this difficult working-memory task [4]. ... this distracting sound thus crucially influences the processes of executive functioning within the brain [12,16] that support the active selection, monitoring and manipulation of information in working memory.

findings.consequent: susceptibility to disruption by auditory distraction
findings.quote: The 10% decrease in baseline performance (6 digits: 93% correct, compared with 8 digits: 83% correct) on this more difficult task might be one of the reasons why this task was more susceptible to disruption.

findings.consequent: disruption of working-memory performance (regardless of visual-verbal vs. visual-spatial content of remembered material)
findings.quote: Changing-state disruption of working-memory peformance occurs not only with to-be-remembered material of visual-verbal content... but also with material of visual-spatial content... Seemingly then, auditory distraction is one of process rather than content.

synthesis_conclusions: Auditory distraction, particularly from changing-state sounds, disrupts working memory.
The brain's response to distracting sound is modulated by working memory load.
Under low working memory load, the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and other memory-related regions suppress irrelevant sound processing, preventing performance disruption.
Under high working memory load, changing-state sounds activate the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex, leading to working memory performance disruption.
The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex plays a crucial role in executive functioning and information manipulation in working memory when faced with distraction under high cognitive load.
Auditory distraction's disruptive effect is primarily related to the processing of changing-state information rather than the specific content of the material being remembered.
evidence_gaps: It is unknown if the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is crucial for working-memory disruption when the remembered material is visual-spatial.
It is an open question whether auditory distraction on low-memory-demand tasks is due to an absence of suppression or activation of additional brain mechanisms.

moderators.effect: Higher working memory load increases susceptibility to disruption by auditory distraction, shifting the brain's response from suppression to activation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Easy tasks (6 digits) show suppression and no disruption; difficult tasks (8 digits) show activation and disruption.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Changes in ignored auditory streams disrupt serial recall and other working memory tasks, particularly when the irrelevant sound contains varying acoustic features.
Auditory distraction interferes with the phonological loop or a more general working memory capacity, especially its serial order processing component.
The auditory system automatically segments sound into objects or streams, and changes within these objects, even if ignored, can capture attention and disrupt cognitive processing.
Salient or changing irrelevant stimuli automatically divert attentional resources, leading to performance decrements in concurrent tasks.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper reviews the causal mechanisms by which changes in ignored auditory stimuli disrupt working memory, often involving automatic change detection and attentional capture.

steps.from_construct: Change in ignored auditory stream (e.g., varying tones)
steps.to_construct: Automatic detection of auditory change (e.g., Mismatch Negativity - MMN)
Interference with serial order processing in working memory
Disruption of working memory performance (e.g., serial recall)

environmental_features: irrelevant speech (e.g., single talker, multi-talker babble)
non-speech sounds (e.g., pure tones, white noise, environmental sounds)
changing-state sequences of sounds (e.g., ABAB tone sequences, varying pitch/timbre)
steady-state sounds (e.g., continuous single tone, white noise, repeating single item)
control_conditions: steady-state irrelevant sound (e.g., continuous white noise or repeating single tone)
irrelevant sound with no internal changes or semantic content

instruments_used.name: Serial Recall Task
instruments_used.construct: Verbal working memory capacity, serial order processing
instruments_used.description: Participants are presented with a list of items (e.g., digits, letters) and asked to recall them in the correct order.

instruments_used.name: Mental Arithmetic Task
instruments_used.description: Participants perform arithmetic calculations while being exposed to distracting sounds.

instruments_used.name: EEG/ERP (Mismatch Negativity - MMN)
instruments_used.description: Measures electrical activity in the brain, particularly event-related potentials like MMN, which reflects automatic detection of auditory deviance.

instruments_used.name: fMRI
instruments_used.construct: Brain activity, neural correlates of attention and working memory
instruments_used.description: Measures changes in blood flow to detect brain activity associated with auditory distraction and cognitive tasks.
